body:
AI's Hidden Cost: Your Next Phone Will Be More Expensive

India's smartphone market is feeling the squeeze from an unlikely source — artificial intelligence. As tech giants gobble up memory chips for AI data centers, the resulting shortage has driven up costs for standard memory used in phones, pushing smartphone prices higher and reshaping the world's second-largest handset market.

Smartphone shipments in India fell 10 percent year-over-year in the April-June quarter, marking the steepest June-quarter decline in six years, according to Counterpoint Research. The decline was far more pronounced than in China, where shipments fell just 2 percent.

Budget Buyers Bear the Brunt

The impact has been most devastating at the lower end of the market, where 60 percent of India's smartphone sales are concentrated. Shipments in the sub-₹15,000 (under $150) segment plummeted 45 percent from a year earlier.

"Sub-brands normally have overlaps and shared resources, and you need a minimum base to justify the cut-throat margins. Profitability is the key to deciding market operations," Tarun Pathak, Counterpoint's vice president of research, told TechCrunch.

Smartphone prices in India have risen between 4 and 68 percent depending on the model. Consumers are either upgrading to pricier devices, delaying purchases by stretching replacement cycles to four years, or turning to the secondhand market.

Samsung Gains, Chinese Brands Retreat

Samsung was the only major brand to post shipment growth in Q2, with volumes rising 2 percent year-over-year. Apple saw a 3 percent dip, largely due to supply constraints. Premium buyers proved less sensitive to price hikes, with financing making expensive devices more affordable.

Chinese brands, heavily exposed to entry- and mid-tier segments, saw combined market share fall to its lowest since 2020. OnePlus announced it would stop launching new products in Europe and North America while maintaining its India business — a pattern likely to repeat across other budget brands.

A Double Whammy for Indian Consumers

"For Indian consumers, it is a double whammy as the weaker currency makes imports costlier, which has added to margin pressures for the market players, and they are passing on the cost to the consumer," Kiranjeet Kaur, IDC's associate research director for mobile phones, told TechCrunch.

Memory shortages and elevated smartphone prices are likely to persist until at least the end of 2027, though the pace of price increases should moderate as consumers adjust.

For the Indian diaspora, the ripple effects are tangible — from rising costs of phones sent to family back home to the shifting competitive landscape that Indian tech professionals navigate at chip manufacturers and smartphone companies worldwide.

Sources: TechCrunch, Counterpoint Research, IDC
nri_angle: Rising smartphone prices in India directly affect NRI families purchasing devices for relatives back home.
